---
title: "Human in the loop: safe agent practices"
description: "You decide and review; the agent does the typing. Six practices that keep it that way."
---

A coding agent can read files, run commands and push to GitHub as you. That
is what makes it useful, and it is also why you stay in the loop. **You make
the decisions and review the result; the agent does the typing.** The six
practices below keep it that way. None of them needs special software: most are
a habit, or a line you put in your repository's agent instructions.

::: {.callout-note}
## On this page

- Review every change before it reaches `main`
- Ask the agent to record its intent, and to prove its code works
- Check every new package
- Know what the agent can reach, and what needs your approval
- Keep credentials out of code
- Mark agent-written work as such
:::

## 1 · Review every change before it reaches `main`

Let the agent work on a branch and open a pull request. You read the pull
request, try it if it matters, and merge it yourself. The agent does not push
to `main` and does not merge.

- Tell it so, at the start of the session or in `AGENTS.md`: *"Work on a branch
  and open a pull request. Never push to main, and never merge."*
- Before you merge, ask it to summarize what the pull request changes. If the
  summary surprises you, read the diff more closely.
- "Done" means done being written, not done being checked.

## 2 · Ask for the intent, and for proof that it works

A reviewer, you or another agent, can only check code against what it was
meant to do. Ask the agent to write that down.

- **Comments for the *why*.** Workarounds, non-obvious choices, things that look
  wrong but are deliberate. Not a narration of every line, which makes code
  harder to review.
- **Notes for decisions.** Keep a short `AGENTS.md` with the repository's rules,
  and a notes file for decisions and the evidence behind them. They also help
  the next session, which starts with no memory of this one.
- **Proof by running.** "I read it and it looks right" is not a test. Ask the
  agent to run the code, ideally in a fresh environment that has only the
  packages the repository declares, and to say in the pull request what it ran
  and what it did not.

## 3 · Check every new package

Agents sometimes suggest packages that do not exist, or have a name one letter
off from a real one. Installing the wrong one runs someone else's code on your
account.

- Before the agent installs a package by name (`pip install something`), have it
  confirm the exact name on PyPI, conda-forge or npm, with a maintainer and
  release history that make sense, and tell you why it is needed.
- Prefer packages the project already uses.
- New packages go into the repository's dependency file (`requirements.txt`,
  `environment.yml`) and are listed in the pull request, so you review them with
  the code.

## 4 · Know what the agent can reach, and what needs your approval

- **The hub is the sandbox.** Your agent runs on a cloud server that holds your
  hackathon work, not on your laptop next to your email and documents. That is
  a good place for an agent. Think twice before running one with broad
  permissions on a machine that has sensitive files.
- **Keep the approval prompts on.** Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity all ask
  before running commands they are unsure of. Each also has a mode that skips
  every prompt. Do not use it. Allow routine, read-only commands if the prompts
  slow you down, but keep the prompts for anything that deletes, pushes,
  installs or merges.
- **Some actions always need you:** merging a pull request, deleting a branch or
  repository, force-pushing or rewriting history, deleting files outside the
  project, and installing a new package. Say so in `AGENTS.md`.
- **One repository per session.** Ask the agent to work only in the repository
  it started in, and to ask before touching any other.

## 5 · Keep credentials out of code

- Never paste a key, token or password into a notebook, script or chat that
  ends up in a repository. On the hub, the scratch bucket uses the hub's own
  credentials, so your code needs none.
- Give the agent a credential with the least access that works and an
  expiry date, like the fine-grained GitHub token in
  [Git and GitHub, with an agent](../setup/04-git-with-agent.qmd).
- Your prompts and code go to the company that runs your agent. Check your
  subscription's privacy settings, and do not give the agent data you are not
  allowed to share with that company.

## 6 · Mark agent-written work as such

Say where an agent helped, so reviewers know what they are looking at.

- Ask the agent to end each commit it makes with a co-author line, for example
  `Co-Authored-By: Agent <agent@noreply.invalid>`, and each pull request with a
  line saying it was generated with an AI coding agent.
- Add a short "AI assistance" note to the README: parts of the code were written
  with AI coding agents, and every change was reviewed by a person before it
  was merged.

## Put it in `AGENTS.md`

Most of this fits in a few lines at the top of your repository's `AGENTS.md`,
which Codex and Antigravity read at the start of every session. Claude Code
reads `CLAUDE.md` instead, so add a `CLAUDE.md` holding the single line
`@AGENTS.md`.

```markdown
## Working rules

- Work on a branch and open a pull request. Never push to main; never merge.
- Ask before deleting branches, rewriting history, or touching another repo.
- Before installing a new package, confirm it exists on PyPI or conda-forge,
  say why it is needed, and add it to requirements.txt.
- Comment the why, not the what. Record decisions in agent/notes.md.
- Test by running in a clean environment. Say in the PR what ran and what did not.
- Never write a credential into a tracked file.
- End commits with `Co-Authored-By: Agent <agent@noreply.invalid>`.
```

An instruction is something the agent follows, not something it is forced to
follow. Your review of each pull request is the check that does not depend on
the agent.
